s04.slug: THURSDAY · 2:40 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE COUNTER
body: In the dead hour the Anchor belongs to the pie case. The sun comes in low off the wharf and through the front glass and lays the shadow of the OPEN sign backwards across the linoleum. On the board by the pass somebody has chalked CHOWDER 4.50 and, under it, in another hand, ASK ABOUT THE FISH, which is a warning, not a special. The case, lit from inside for nobody, holds nine pies and one fly that has made up its mind about the lemon meringue. Jack still has the Point on him: salt stiff at his temples, sand in his left ear that he suspects will turn up in Texas. He has done the arithmetic on the way over — tonight and next week’s three shifts, eight dollars an hour, close to two hundred before tips — and it is not a number he enjoys carrying through the door.

Up on the shelf over the register KNX is giving the news to the room. The government has opened an inquiry into the brakes on the Prius. The Colts are favored by six. Dwight Freeney’s ankle gets a minute to itself, the way a head of state’s would. “Used to be a brake was something you pushed,” Merle says. He is the only customer, and he has been saying things to chowder since before Jack was hired. “I’ll take the Saints and the points,” he adds, unprompted.

Gloria is behind the case with a bar towel over one shoulder and a grease pencil stuck in her hair, giving each pie its quarter-turn so none of them takes the sun. She doesn’t look up for the bell over the door.
“Your roommate came in Tuesday,” she says, to the apple. “Asked me for you.”
“Gloria —”

“He had a speech. I let him finish; it had a structure. One, you’re reliable. Two, you’ve never asked anyone for anything. Three, the Saints. I asked which ones. The callback was to a pie.” The apple gets its quarter. “Then I told him it wasn’t his to ask.” She moves down the case and gives the lemon meringue the same. “Meringue, your roommate. All lift. Leave him out in the damp and he weeps.”
“I didn’t say yes till last night. I didn’t know about Tuesday —”
“Hands.” She still hasn’t turned. “You ask a woman for a thing, you stand up and say it to her face. Not to the pie.”
He is already standing. He takes his hands out of his pockets anyway, and that seems to be what she meant.

“I need tonight,” he says. “And next week, all of it. I’m going to New Orleans tomorrow, five in the morning, in a minivan, thirty hours, with five other people, and I should have called you this morning, and I’m asking now.”
Gloria turns around. She looks at him until Merle’s spoon stops: the salt, the ear, the sunburn coming up across his nose, whatever his face has been doing since September.
“There he is,” she says, to the face and not to anything he asked.
“Where was I?”
“Closing time,” Gloria says. “Since about December. What’s in New Orleans?”
“The Saints.”
“The game’s in Miami.”
“The city’s where you watch it.”
“Uh-huh,” Gloria says. Then it’s business. “Hector has tonight and next week. He’s got a baby six weeks old. He’ll take every hour you’ve got and ask for the ones you don’t.”
“I’ll make it up to him.”
“He’ll let you. Don’t be nice about it.” The towel comes off one shoulder and goes onto the other. “Six of you in a minivan. Somebody cries by Phoenix.”
“Tucson,” says Merle. “Everybody cries in Tucson.”
“Your professor had the back booth Saturday till close,” Gloria says. “You were off.”
“I know.”
“Told me his dog had a difficult evening.” The lemon meringue gets another eighth of a turn, which it did not need. “In front of the *dog*, hon?”
“What dog?” says Merle.
“Eat your chowder, Merle.”
Jack has an answer ready for the next question, which is who started it. Gloria goes to the register instead.

From the shelf under it she brings out the share jar, a gallon pickle jar with SHARE on a strip of masking tape, and counts his portion onto the counter in ones and fives, wetting her thumb on every fifth bill. It goes into a plain envelope. Across the front, in the grease pencil, she prints COSTIGAN, and she folds the flap down and then the envelope over twice.
“Through Sunday,” she says. “It’s early. Don’t make anything of it.”
“It’s not due till —”
“It’s due when I say.” She holds it out until he takes it. It is thicker than his share. He can tell by the weight, a week and a half in a week’s envelope, and he opens his mouth.
“Don’t count it in front of me,” Gloria says. “Count it in Texas. And don’t send me a postcard. Thirty years on my feet, I’ve been as far as Bakersfield. I don’t want to be told what it looks like.”

Back past the pass the Hobart finishes its cycle with a groan, and in the quiet Rudy speaks without turning from the sink, the rosary on his wrist swinging with the rack. He has had the date since Jack mentioned it once, over the steam, to the one man in the building who would know what to do with it.
“Your brother,” Rudy says. “The birthday.”
“He called.”
“Good.”
The Hobart starts up again. Jack puts the envelope in his shirt pocket.
“Lena’s grandmother called me this morning,” he says. “She says don’t bring anything.”
“And you believed her.”
“She’s eighty-eight.”

“That’s how you get to eighty-eight. You tell people not to bring anything and you keep count of who listened.” Gloria wipes her hands on the towel. “Thirty years I’ve watched people carry my pies out that door. Three ways. Out in front, like an apology. Low, like a bribe. Level, both hands, like the floor’s wet and somebody’s mother is watching.” “You haven’t got a pie and you’re already carrying it level.”
“Gloria.”
“You don’t walk into somebody’s house empty-handed. I don’t care whose. Cream is done by Blythe. Meringue weeps, you’ve met one. Apple wants a plate and a person to hold it. You pick.”

She steps aside from the case, which she does not do for the other customers, and gives him all of it: the lemon meringue; the coconut cream; the apple under its lattice, which he has been told is him; the boysenberry, bleeding purple into its tin; the pecan, the top gone dark and glossy and studded to the edge. Jack knows what Gloria calls the people he knows, pie by pie, and she has not been wrong yet. She isn’t watching him look. She is watching the case, the grease pencil back in her hand, giving him nothing.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’ Thursday I asked her for Saturday night. ‘Who’s she?’ ‘You met her.’ ‘Boysenberry.’ She gave it to Rudy’s nephew. Her granddaughter got her watching *Sweetwater*; Thursdays at nine, for the clothes. She rated Cassidy a vanilla custard. Skye agreed. Thursday I asked her for the trip. Theo asked her Tuesday; she told him it wasn’t his to ask. Hector has my shifts — the baby’s six weeks. She counted my tips out early into an envelope with my name on it in grease pencil. Hale told her about the dog. In front of the dog. She made me pick the pie for the Broussards.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’ Opened the walk-in on me Tuesday. ‘Mijo. Lettuce.’ Took the lettuce himself. Tuesday, over the Hobart: come hear my mother sing at the Mission, Saturday, five a.m. She came up from Oxnard for the Virgin and sang every verse with her eyes shut. Thursday from the dish pit: your brother, the birthday. He called. Good.

choices.key: At the Anchor you picked the Broussards’ pie: pecan. It travels — Gloria’s own words, back at her.
response: Gloria hears it come back across the counter. “Mm.”

She lifts the pecan out by its tin, sets it on a white box and brings the flaps up around it, fast, an old hand. The grease pencil comes out of her hair. On the lid, in the capitals she uses for everything in that kitchen, she writes a 5 and rings it. “Not on the floor of that van,” she says. “A pie on a floor mat has a bad trip. Somebody holds it. Somebody with a lap.” She runs the red-and-white string around twice and pulls it tight in one pull.

choices.key: At the Anchor you picked the Broussards’ pie: boysenberry. Gloria said it stains.
response: “It stains,” Gloria says. The pie is already out of its tin and onto a square of wax paper; the ones that run get wax paper.

She builds the box around it, quick and square, and looks at him once. “Mm.” Then: “Keep it off anything white. Keep it off anything you like.” On the lid she writes a 5, rings it, and parks the pencil back in her hair, behind her ear.

choices.key: At the Anchor you let Gloria pick the Broussards’ pie. She boxed the pecan without a word.
response: Gloria’s hand is on the pecan’s tin before he has finished the sentence. She boxes it with her back half turned, so that the lid is her business, and the pencil goes across it once and then round. Then she slides the box the length of the counter, past the napkins and the sugars, and it stops, level, against his hands.

s05.slug: THURSDAY · 4:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS — FRANK
body: Delgado’s front steps keep the day’s last warm stone. Jack has the third one to himself, the pie box level across his knees, the long light coming sideways through the eucalyptus, and the RAZR on the step beside him, where it is not expected to do anything. Down the walk a girl in a Pi Lam sweatshirt hauls a laundry bag toward the door by both its ears.
It goes off. The outside screen says DAD.
He lets it ring twice, out of something close to fear, and then opens it. “Pop? What’s wrong?”
“Nothing’s wrong.” On Glenwood Avenue a radio is on low, a man explaining LeBron James at some length. “Can’t I call.”
“You never call.”
“So I’m calling.”
“Where are you?”
“Garage. Truck door’s open, I got the radio.” A boot turns on concrete. “Your mother says you’re going to New Orleans.”
“Yeah.”
“For the Saints.”
“Yeah.”
“…Good.”
“I went to the bank,” Frank says. “Market Street. There’s sixty dollars in your account. For gas.”
Sixty dollars is gas for the Silverado to Pittsburgh and back three times. Jack does the sum before he can stop himself, and he knows his father did it first, at the window, with somebody watching.
“Pop —”
“Sixty. A hundred’s showing off.”
“Pop. With everything, you can’t just —”
“Cruze line, next year,” Frank says. “Maybe.” The radio goes to a mattress commercial. “It ain’t a question.”
“The girl at the window said that was a nice thing to do for somebody.” The boot again. “I told her it’s gas.”
Against his chest, in the shirt pocket, the Anchor’s envelope. Two people have counted money out for him today, and neither would let him watch.
“Your roommate e-mailed your mother a budget.”
“Theo did?”
“Dear Mrs. Costigan. With a chart. A pie chart.” Frank gives that its due. “I said what’s the pie. Your mother said it’s a kind of graph. Gas, forty-one percent. Food. A slice called Contingency.”
“What’s Contingency?”

“Your mother says it’s for if he’s wrong. Down the bottom it says Yours in transit. I said what’s that. She said it’s how rich people sign.” Something clinks onto the bench. “Sixty-one dollars a head. She printed it. It’s on the refrigerator under St. Joseph.”
“Pop —”
“Sixty is a number,” Frank says. “Sixty-one is a man who rounded up. The kid said sixty-one. You find the dollar.”

body.text: “Your grandmother’s telling the whole Altar Society the TV one’s got range. I don’t know what that means and I’m not asking.”

body: “Hold on.” Paper rustles on the bench, folded small. “Your mother wrote it down.”

“Gina wants footage. I said he don’t have the camera. She said he has a phone. I said that phone shoots like a potato.” The paper again. “Rosie wants the crabs. A report. She gave your mother a list in Latin, I’m not reading it.”
“Callinectes sapidus.”

“That.” Frank does not sound sorry he asked. “Your mother lit the St. Joseph candle in the kitchen for the trip. I said it’s a car, not a war. She said St. Joseph doesn’t know the difference and neither does she.” The paper goes back into a pocket. “That was hers. The rest is me.”
“What is it, a Honda?”
“An Odyssey. It’s Kevin’s mother’s.”
“Honda makes a motor. Have him check the oil at the Arizona line. Who’s driving?”
“Kevin first. Then me, through Texas.”
“Kevin any good?”
“He’s pre-med. He drives like there’s a patient in the back.”
“That’s a driver. Texas is the long one. You remember Nebraska.”
“Pop, I remember Nebraska.”
“Texas is Nebraska with a flag. You get tired, you pull over before you think you have to. Sleeping’s free. I checked.”
“Okay.”
“What’s it down there, sixty?”
“Sixty-two, they said.”
“In February. That’s not weather. That’s a sales pitch. Here it’s nine. Truck’s got a block heater and a bad attitude.”
“Colts by six, they say.”
“They say.” Frank has opinions about this. “Manning I don’t like. Man changes the play at the line. A play’s a play. You call it, you run it.”
“He’s good at it, Pop.”
“That’s what I don’t like. You watching it down there?”
“Sunday. Yeah.”
“Watch it with people. That’s the whole thing. You don’t watch it by yourself.”
“I won’t.”
“And you look at the river. The Mississippi. I never saw that one. I saw the —” He clears his throat. “The Pacific. It was big. I looked at it a while. It’s allowed.”
“Okay, Pop.”
“And tell the TV one your mother says Canada’s cold.”

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.” Asked me what it’s like in there. Went in on Holy Family Sunday — his name was on the list at the desk; he asked Ma where he’s supposed to stand. Told Danny about the hall and the Cruze, and laughed, in there. Asked if the Saints girl sent the coffee. I said yeah. Told Danny they wouldn’t lose. Three straight. His phone died in the cold and he borrowed mine. New Year’s: a ginger ale, in a glass. New Year’s: two spoons of lentils, for the money. “Pryor.” Went in to see Danny again. “Four straight.” Twelfth Night we took the lights down, and the beer fridge is ginger ale now. At the curb in Pittsburgh: call your mother when you land. She don’t sleep. Thursday he called me — him, not Ma. He put sixty dollars in my account for gas. It ain’t a question. Theo e-mailed Ma a budget, with a chart. Watch it with people, he says; that’s the whole thing. Tell the TV one Ma says Canada’s cold.

choices.key: Your father put sixty dollars in your account for gas. You said thanks, Pop. He said yeah.
response: “Your mother wants to know did you eat. I’m not asking.”
“I’ll tell her you said so.” The radio goes on with its business. On Glenwood Avenue the garage door’s chain starts to run, up for the cold air or down for the night; from here Jack can’t tell which.

choices.key: Your father put sixty dollars in your account for gas. You told him to put it on Danny’s books instead. He left yours where it was.
response: A can goes down on the workbench, hard enough to ring. “Your brother’s got money,” Frank says. The radio fills the space where the rest of it would go. “Your brother’s got more money than you.”
The sixty stays where it is. When he says goodnight he says, “I got to be at Market Street when it opens. That girl’s going to put me in her will.”

choices.text: “I’ve got it, Pop. I’ve got tips.”
choices.key: Your father put sixty dollars in your account for gas. You told him you’ve got tips. It ain’t a question, he said — twice.
response: “It ain’t a question.” Flatter this time, and final. “Keep the tips for the way home.”
The truck door thunks shut at his end, close to the phone, and the radio goes small behind the glass.
